2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.

Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable: the study runs a deterministic 12-month computational simulation in NetLogo v4.1.3 using static secondary summary inputs rather than following a cohort or panel of human participants over time.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: the deterministic simulation attributes cross-system differences in water service delivery (WSD) performance solely to principal-agent game equilibria and calibrates a single free parameter C (1.6 in Kenya; 1.8 in Ghana) against country-average performance scores, omitting infrastructural, hydrological, fiscal, tariff, and demographic confounders between Kenyan and Ghanaian urban service areas.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak: regulatory and contractual frameworks in Kenya (MWI, WASREB, municipal corporate utilities) and Ghana (MHWW, PURC, GWCL, AVRL management contract) are stylized into dyadic principal-agent links scored on a coarse 3-point ordinal transparency scale (0, 0.5, 1 for written rules) and accountability scale without citing specific statutes, regulations, licenses, or contract provisions.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: governance inputs (transparency, accountability, participation [TAP], and social cost) and WSD performance benchmarks rely on secondary 'participatory scoring' imported from prior reports (GII 2011; TIK 2011; Bellaubi and Visscher 2014) plus 'Bellaubi (personal observation)' (PDF p. 3), with no primary measurement protocols, respondent counts, or inter-rater reliability reported here; additionally, Table 3 (PDF p. 3) swaps the text definitions and unit scales of Continuity and Coverage, and Table 5 (PDF p. 7) states a maximum indicator value of 3 (total 15) despite Table 3 defining 0-2 scales (maximum total 10).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak (secondary coarse benchmark): WSD performance is imported from five previously studied urban neighbourhoods as a 5-indicator ordinal WSDA score (continuity, quality, coverage, affordability, quantity; Tables 3 and 5) containing internal definitional/scale discrepancies between Tables 3 and 5 and collapsed into unweighted country means (23.3% in Kenya; 16.6% in Ghana) to calibrate simulated game payoffs.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: model code and ODD documentation are deposited externally in the CoMSES Computational Model Library (Bellaubi et al. 2014), supporting computational inspectability, but the paper reports no pre-specified analysis/validation plan, no sensitivity analysis to ad hoc payoff equations (e.g., T = 1.5 - accountability; S = (participation / C) - social cost), and calibrates one free parameter per country against a single country-level mean percentage.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern in secondary empirical inputs (not directly applicable to deterministic simulation mechanics): calibration relies on five pre-existing urban case-study neighbourhoods (Old Town in Mombasa, Migosi in Kisumu, and Kangemi in Nairobi, Kenya; Madina and Nima in Accra, Ghana) from Bellaubi and Visscher (2014), with no sampling frame, site-selection rationale, or household/informant recruitment criteria reported in this article.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Bellaubi and Pahl-Wostl (2017) present a deterministic, game-theoretic agent-based model (ABM) implemented in NetLogo v4.1.3 to explore how corruption risks (operationalized via transparency, accountability, participation [TAP], and social cost/gain scores) and management practices (opportunistic vs. pragmatic) shape urban water service delivery (WSD) performance in Kenya and Ghana. Because the paper conducts a computational social simulation parameterized and calibrated with pre-existing summary scores from five previously published urban case studies (Bellaubi and Visscher 2014, 2016; GII 2011; TIK 2011) rather than primary empirical data collection, doctrinal/jurimetric legal analysis, or a systematic review, no listed risk-of-bias checklist applies (chosen_tool = NONE). Methodologically, depositing the model's ODD documentation in the CoMSES library (Bellaubi et al. 2014) supports computational transparency. However, substantial evidentiary limitations constrain empirical and causal inference: (1) all TAP, social-cost, and WSDA performance inputs are imported from secondary 'participatory scoring' and 'personal observation' without primary sampling, coding, or reliability details in this text; (2) Table 3 swaps the definitions and measurement units of Continuity and Coverage, and Table 5 cites a maximum indicator score of 3 (total 15) that contradicts Table 3's 0-2 scoring scale; (3) payoff functional forms (e.g., T = 1.5 - accountability; S = (participation / C) - social cost) and sequential move order (agent always moving first, preventing shifting Cd/Dc dynamics at the consumption level; PDF p. 12) are imposed by assumption without structural sensitivity testing; and (4) calibration tunes one free parameter C per country (1.6 in Kenya; 1.8 in Ghana) to match a single unweighted country-mean WSDA score (23.3% across 3 Kenyan sites; 16.6% across 2 Ghanaian sites), providing no independent out-of-sample validation and leaving physical, financial, and hydrological confounders unmodeled.

raw_response.where_found_summary: Abstract & Introduction (PDF pp. 1-2); Research Methodology & secondary case-study sourcing (PDF p. 2); Principal-agent TAP, management practice, and WSDA indicator definitions and Kenya/Ghana actor mappings (PDF pp. 2-7, Tables 1-5, Figs. 1-2); NetLogo v4.1.3 ABM specification, payoff equations, and sequential decision/learning rules (PDF pp. 4, 7-8, Figs. 3-4, Table 6); Single principal-agent equilibrium dynamics, calibration of parameter C, and country simulation outputs (PDF pp. 9-12, Figs. 5-10, Table 7); Discussion and model limitations (PDF p. 12).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: This article develops and runs a deterministic computational simulation—an agent-based model (ABM) in NetLogo v4.1.3 built on game-theoretic payoff matrices and bounded-rational learning equations—parameterized and calibrated against pre-existing aggregate ordinal scores from prior publications (Bellaubi and Visscher 2014, 2016; GII 2011; TIK 2011). It reports no primary empirical human-subjects sampling, survey/cohort data collection, quasi-experimental policy evaluation, primary qualitative fieldwork, mixed-methods primary integration, systematic literature search, or doctrinal/jurimetric analysis of primary legal texts. Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, forcing a primary empirical checklist or the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework onto a computational simulation model is inappropriate, so NONE is selected.
